transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-09
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Omar (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SA), Liam (Cygnus ML), Nora (Cygnus Infra), Ben (Cygnus SRE), Aisha (Cygnus Research)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, I see Liam, Nora, Ben, Aisha, Omar, Priya. Cool. The plan for today is a deep technical dive on quantization options - INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ - and how they affect runtime perf and accuracy for your 13B/30B models. We'll also touch on KV cache and on-prem/VPC constraints.

[00:24] Liam: Sounds good, high level we care about keeping production latency under 120ms p95 for generation up to 256 tokens and no more than 3% accuracy regression on our NLU tasks. We run both 13B and 30B variants in different pipelines.

[00:40] Omar: Got it. Quick question on your pipelines - are you currently using any quantized models in prod or is everything FP16?

[00:48] Aisha: Mostly FP16 in prod. We've experiment with FP8 internal labs but haven't shipped it. GPTQ runs looked promising but we saw some weird hallucination patterns on a subset of prompts.

[01:05] Priya: Thanks. We'll try to unpack that. Just to flag: when we talk about AWQ here that's referring to asymmetric weight quantization library runs, not another Redwood feature. Sometimes the transcription or notes call it A-WQ or AWQ-lib, you'll see slight naming differences in our docs.

[01:22] Nora: Also to confirm, our infra preference is VPC with peered dedicated cluster for the pilot - we need KMS integration and audit logs.

[01:30] Maya: Noted. We'll include the security checklist. Omar, can you kick off with the INT8 vs FP8 baseline?

[01:36] Omar: Sure. High level: INT8 gives the best memory reduction and often best throughput on GPU when kernels are optimized for INT8 math. However, INT8 tends to be more brittle for certain attention layers and normalization; you see per-token score shifts that can translate to accuracy regression on some tasks. FP8 - more recent - gives a middle ground: smaller memory than FP16 but retains more dynamic range, so fewer regressions. The caveat: FP8 requires runtime and compiler support - we've been shipping FP8 in our dedicated runtime when backend supports it, but tooling maturity varies across hardware.

[02:25] Liam: For our 13B model, what's typical p95 latency delta when moving from FP16 to INT8 vs FP8? ballpark numbers?

[02:33] Omar: Ballpark on an A100-class GPU: FP16 baseline p95 for 256 tokens is ~90-110ms depending on batching; INT8 optimized path can drop that to ~65-80ms, FP8 is usually ~75-95ms. There's variation depending on kernel selection, KV cache hits, and batching strategy. On H100, the deltas compress a bit because newer kernels are faster for FP16 and FP8.

[03:05] Ben: How does KV cache play into that? Our sessions are mostly conversational so we rely heavily on prefix caching.

[03:12] Omar: Great question. KV cache memory footprint reduces with quantization, so INT8 can reduce cache pressure significantly which helps latency at high concurrency. But there's an implementation detail: if KV cache is stored or transmitted in FP16 and the model weights are INT8, we still pay serialization cost. Redwood's runtime supports on-GPU KV cache in quantized formats to avoid round-trip conversions, but that requires model conversion steps. In practice we see a 10-25% latency improvement at 95th when cache hit rates are high with INT8.

[03:55] Aisha: We noticed hallucination spikes in GPTQ runs - you mentioned brittleness for INT8, what about GPTQ specifically?

[04:03] Omar: GPTQ is a post-training quantization method that groups weights to preserve distribution; it's great for extreme compression, like 4-bit. For LLMs, GPTQ often preserves downstream metrics better than naive symmetric quant, but it can still create outlier errors on rare tokens or long-context tasks because it optimizes for distribution-wide MSE rather than worst-case logits. AWQ has different rounding heuristics and has been shown in some papers to reduce those outliers. But neither is perfect; you want to validate on your eval set.

[04:45] Liam: So AWQ vs GPTQ - which do you recommend we start production pilot with?

[04:50] Omar: For your use case, I'd recommend running both in our benchmark harness. AWQ tends to be safer for 8-bit-ish regimes and gives decent latency wins with fewer regressions; GPTQ is compelling if you want 4-bit extreme compression but you'll need more eval coverage. We typically do a staged approach: AWQ for initial pilot, GPTQ for an aggressive cost trial if metrics hold.

[05:12] Priya: Important to highlight kernel support: some runtimes ship hardware-specific fused attention kernels optimized for FP16 or FP8, but for INT8/GPTQ you might rely on fallback kernels which can reduce throughput. Redwood's runtime does automatic kernel selection based on model shape, seq len, and hardware.

[05:36] Nora: For VPC/on-prem, are there any restrictions on running AWQ/GPTQ? I mean, is the conversion done client-side or in Redwood's control plane?

[05:45] Maya: Good point. For Private deployments we can ship conversion tools that you run in your environment, so weights never leave your network. For hosted/Dedicated we can do conversion in a controlled job with customer consent. We'll document the flow clearly.

[05:58] Ben: What about retraining or fine-tuning after quantization? We do some small ft for customization.

[06:05] Omar: Quantization-aware fine-tuning is possible but more complex. With INT8/AWQ you usually fine-tune in FP16 then quantize; there are QAT pipelines for INT8/FP8 but they add churn. For most customers we recommend domain-tuning pre-quantization and then verifying. If you need continuous online fine-tuning, we'd suggest keeping a FP16 path for training and a quantized path for serving, with periodic re-quantization after updates.

[06:38] Aisha: Can you speak to typical accuracy regressions? We flagged a 3-5% drop on one classification eval with GPTQ.

[06:46] Omar: Numbers vary but rough guidance: AWQ/INT8 in many models gives 0-2% regression on classification/QA tasks; GPTQ at 4-bit can be 2-8% on some sensitive metrics. FP8 often sits around 0-1% regression but depends on model and eval. That's why we run per-customer evals. Also, some failure modes are distributional - e.g., long-tail prompt types or tokenization edge cases.

[07:20] Liam: Ok. On benchmarking methodology: how do you recommend we run tests so the numbers are meaningful for us?

[07:26] Priya: We recommend three axes: latency/throughput bench with synthetic representative workloads (varying seq len), regression pass on your labeled eval set (we'll run exact-match/F1/ROUGE etc), and an adversarial prompt set for hallucination/regression detection. We'll run each quantization method with identical batching and KV cache settings and surface diffs using logits and top-k outputs.

[07:53] Nora: About batching - we expect high concurrency during peak and low at night. How does batching strategy differ for quantized models?

[08:02] Omar: Quantized models benefit from larger batch sizes due to improved GPU utilization, but batching increases latency tail. For conversational workloads with tight p95 SLOs, we use dynamic batching with timeouts and early dispatch for small interactive requests. INT8 often lets you increase concurrency because of memory savings. We also use shard-level batching for multi-tenant pools.

[08:30] Ben: Any specific kernel or compiler flags we should be aware of when running on H100 vs A100?

[08:36] Omar: On H100 enable the newer tensor core FP8 paths if you're using FP8; for INT8 tune the cuBLAS/cublasLt selection and make sure your runtime uses fused MHA kernels. Redwood's runtime auto-selects but if you run raw it helps to set cuBLAS config like gemm algo heuristics. We'll share recommended flags in the benchmark doc.

[08:58] Aisha: You mentioned serialization of KV cache earlier. Is there a best practice for our session store? We use Redis off-host for durability.

[09:07] Omar: For low latency conversational apps, on-GPU KV cache is ideal. With Redis you incur network hop; quantization reduces data size but network RTT dominates. If you stick with Redis for durability, use delta diffs and keep hot sessions pinned to dedicated nodes or use Redis on the same VPC with high-throughput NICs. For on-prem pilot, colocating Redis and GPU nodes yields best p95.

[09:35] Liam: What about instrumentation? We need token-level cost breakdowns and debugging traces when regressions happen.

[09:43] Priya: Redwood Console provides token-level cost and latency breakdowns plus model diff tooling. For regressions we create pairwise diffs on token logits and backtrace to a contributing layer. We'll show an example in the benchmark results.

[09:58] Nora: One of our security folks asked about KMS/HSM integration for private deployments. Any constraints when doing conversion or running quantized models?

[10:06] Maya: The conversion step only touches weights - keys and configs are separate. For Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key management, and audit logs are generated locally. We can run conversions in your VPC so nothing leaves the boundary.

[10:20] Ben: Can we see a sample of the benchmark artifact? What columns and metrics do you include?

[10:26] Omar: Yes. Typical artifact: model, quantization_method, seq_len, batch_size, kv_cache_hit_rate, p50, p95, throughput (tokens/sec), GPU_mem_used, accuracy_metrics (F1/EM), hallucination_flag_rate, notes. We'll share a spreadsheet.

[10:41] Liam: Great. Any gotchas you commonly see with customer models?

[10:45] Omar: Two common issues: tokenization sensitivity and layernorm quant sensitivity. Tokenization causes big diffs if your prompt preprocessing changes token boundaries; make sure you're using identical tokenizer versions. Layernorm in older model variants can be sensitive - sometimes you need per-layer outlier clipping or k-means based quant clustering to stabilize.

[11:05] Aisha: About outlier clipping - is that part of AWQ or an additional pre-step?

[11:10] Omar: Both. AWQ implementations often incorporate outlier handling; GPTQ pipelines sometimes include explicit outlier detection and per-channel scaling. We'll include config snippets.

[11:22] Maya: Quick recap and concrete next steps: Redwood to run AWQ and GPTQ benches on our side for 13B and 30B with the config Omar mentioned; Cygnus to provide eval set and VPC peering info; schedule a 2-hour run mid next week. Action items are in the notes. Anything else?

[11:40] Nora: One last ask - can you include a short note on rollback strategies if quantized model causes regressions?

[11:47] Priya: Sure. Rollback strategies: keep FP16 as canary, use canary split traffic, automated monitor thresholds (latency and key metrics) to auto-failover, and keep model diffs to quickly identify where the regression is. We'll add a one-pager.

[11:59] Liam: Perfect. Thanks all.

[12:05] Maya: Thank you, we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and schedule.

End of call.
